opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so one of the nice things about LEACE is that the eraser itself is just an affine transformation. You compute it in closed form from the class-conditional means and the covariance of the representations, and what you get out is basically a projection, in a whitened coordinate system, that guarantees no linear classifier can do better than chance at predicting the concept from the erased representation, while changing the representation as little as possible in a least-squares sense.

Because it's affine, you don't need to keep it around as a separate module at inference time. You can fold it directly into the weights of an adjacent linear layer. If you have a linear map right after the point where you erase, you just multiply the eraser matrix into that weight matrix and adjust the bias. So you end up with a model that has the same architecture, the same number of parameters, and no extra inference cost, but the concept has been surgically removed at that point in the network.

The more interesting question is where you apply it. If you erase at a single layer, the downstream layers can sometimes reconstruct the information nonlinearly, because LEACE only guarantees linear guardedness. So in the paper we proposed a procedure we called concept scrubbing, where you go through the network layer by layer. You fit an eraser on the residual stream at layer one, apply it, then run the data forward through the already-erased network to get the new representations at layer two, fit an eraser there, and so on. Each eraser is fit on the representations as they actually exist after the earlier erasures, which matters because the statistics shift once you've intervened upstream.

You can then imagine using this for things like fairness, removing a protected attribute so the model can't linearly use it, or as an interpretability tool. In that framing it's more of a scientific instrument: if I erase the representation of, say, part of speech, how much does the model's loss go up? That gives you a causal measure of how much the model relies on linearly available information about that concept, which is a lot more informative than just training a probe and seeing that the information is decodable.

I'd add a caveat, though. I don't think it's a complete solution for safety-critical erasure, precisely because the guarantee is linear. If you need to make sure a model really can't use some information in any way, you'd want stronger methods, possibly nonlinear erasure or erasure combined with fine-tuning. But as a cheap, provably minimal, closed-form intervention that you can bake straight into the weights, I think it's a really useful building block.

r001.rationale: It says the affine eraser can be folded into an adjacent linear layer’s weights, but does not describe this as a low-rank update.

r002.rationale: It describes the eraser as a projection in whitened coordinates, but does not identify it as a low-rank perturbation of the identity matrix.

r003.rationale: It proposes fitting erasers layer by layer after earlier erasures, but does not propose repeatedly updating the erasure transformation throughout training to track changing representations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that LEACE, at its core, is just a linear map. It's an affine transformation that you apply to a representation, and it's provably the least-destructive such transformation that makes a concept linearly undetectable. So the question of how you incorporate it into a model is actually pretty natural, because a transformer is already mostly a stack of linear maps with some nonlinearities sprinkled in between.

The most direct approach is what we did in the paper, which we called concept scrubbing. You go layer by layer, you fit the eraser on the residual stream activations at that layer, and then you apply it to the activations before they get passed to the next layer. And you have to do this sequentially, because once you've erased the concept at layer one, the activations at layer two change, so you have to refit. The nice thing is that because it's just an affine map, you can literally fold it into the weights. The projection and the bias term can be absorbed into the following linear layer, so at inference time there's essentially no overhead. You're not running some auxiliary network, you're not doing anything expensive. You've just changed the weights slightly.

Now, there's a subtlety here that I think is important. LEACE gives you a guarantee about linear detectability. It says no linear classifier can recover the concept from these representations better than chance. But it doesn't say anything about nonlinear detectability. And when you apply it at every layer, the layers in between are nonlinear, so in principle the concept can get re-encoded in some nonlinear way that a later eraser then picks up and removes again. That's actually part of why the layer-by-layer approach works reasonably well in practice. You're repeatedly knocking it down.

The thing I find more interesting, though, is using it during training rather than just as a post-hoc intervention. If you're training a model and you want it to not rely on some feature, say gender in a hiring context or some spurious correlation in your data, you can insert the eraser as a fixed layer and let the gradients flow through it. The model then learns to solve the task in a way that's compatible with that concept being absent, rather than learning it and then having you rip it out afterward, which tends to hurt performance more. There's a difference between amputating something and never growing it in the first place.

And honestly, part of what motivates me here is interpretability. If you have a provable guarantee that a concept isn't linearly present, and the model still does the task fine, that tells you something real about whether the model actually needed that concept. That's a stronger kind of evidence than probing alone gives you, because probing only tells you a concept is there, not whether it's being used. Erasure lets you do the counterfactual.

r001.rationale: The response says the affine eraser can be folded into a following linear layer, but does not state that incorporating it into an already trained model uses a low-rank weight update.

r002.rationale: It describes LEACE as an affine transformation, but does not identify it as a low-rank perturbation of the identity matrix.

r003.rationale: It proposes inserting a fixed eraser during training; it does not say the erasure transformation is repeatedly updated to track changing representations.

astra-6.text:
I think the most straightforward way is to make the erasure operation part of the model’s forward pass. You take an intermediate representation, apply a transformation that removes the linearly accessible information about the concept you care about, and then pass that representation to the rest of the network.

The interesting question is where you put that operation. If you do it at one layer, later layers may reconstruct the information from other features. So you could imagine applying it at multiple points, or training with the erasure operation in place so that the model learns to perform its task under that constraint.

But I’d distinguish that from saying the model no longer knows the concept. Removing linear access to information is a specific condition; it doesn’t guarantee that a nonlinear computation can’t recover it, or that the model’s behavior is independent of it.

r002.rationale: It describes a transformation that removes linearly accessible information, but does not identify it as a low-rank perturbation of the identity matrix.

r003.rationale: It mentions training with the erasure operation in place, but does not say to repeatedly update the transformation to track changing representations.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to do it is to insert a LEACE projection into the model’s forward pass. You choose a particular layer, estimate the relationship between its activations and the concept you want to erase, and then apply an affine transformation that makes that concept linearly unpredictable from those activations.

You could leave that transformation in place as a layer, or, where the architecture allows it, fold it into an adjacent linear layer. You can also apply erasure at multiple layers, because removing a concept at one point doesn’t prevent later layers from reconstructing it from other information.

The important qualification is that the guarantee is about linear predictability. It doesn’t mean the model has completely forgotten the concept, or that no nonlinear computation could recover it. But it gives you a fairly precise intervention for studying how the model uses that information.

r001.rationale: The response describes inserting a projection into a model and possibly folding it into an adjacent linear layer, but does not state that this is a low-rank weight update to an already trained model.

r002.rationale: It describes an affine transformation, but does not identify it as a low-rank perturbation of the identity matrix.

r003.rationale: It suggests applying erasure at multiple layers, but does not propose applying it throughout training or repeatedly updating the transformation as representations change.
